Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Carl sat chewing, his glasses balanced on the very tip of his nose. He was concentrating very hard. Cass watched fascinated. One more chew and they would slip off. "Well," Carl lifted his head and his glasses slid back into place. "I don't know if we can do anything more, Cass. If adults can't stop them, what can we do?"

The twins ate in silence, watching the sun slip behind the distant skyline, silhouetting the tall faceless office blocks that poked out of a shifting yellow haze. The din of the city traffic barely reached them. It mingled with the warm shushing sound of the surrounding park.

The Trumper Tree rose above them, majestic and tall, its twisted branches and gnarled trunk swirling in strange patterns. It looked as if it reached into the sky forever.

"I'm going to save a leaf from the Trumper Tree as a memento," said Cass and she picked up a fallen leaf. "Here's one for you," and she handed it to Carl. He was very quiet. The air became heavy and still. The park seemed to be holding its breath.

"Let's make a wish, a wish to make things right," whispered Cass.

"I don't believe in wishes," was Carl's reply, but he didn't push the leaf away; he placed it carefully in his pocket.

Around them the valley waited, motionless and silent. Cass shivered. "I feel strange, eerie. I can almost hear the tree speaking to me."

"What am I supposed to listen for?"

"Quiet! Can't you hear? There's a sound in the leaves, a sort of stirring, a movement, a rustling."

"And for your next trick there'll be gnomes in the grass." Carl was not impressed.

Cass was listening intently. "It's saying that now is the time, now is special, if we wish now something important will happen."

"And pigs might fly. Come on Cass, it's time we went home."

"Please let's try one wish now. Come on Carl, please...!"

"Oh, all right. Just one, then we must go or Mum and Dad will be late for that meeting."

"Let's put our arms around the tree and wish hard for something to save it."

AnswerA: arguing with his sister
AnswerB: hiding from his parents
AnswerC: quickly finishing a big meal

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
The latest Tyranno movie, Tyranno 2: Earth defence, has just taken a nosedive and crash-landed at a cinema near you all in 3D! While the original Tyranno was a visual feast with strong characters and a gripping story, Tyranno 2 has failed miserably as so many sequels do. It is loosely based on the second book in the excellent series by Lillian Sidle, but it has mutated into a truly awful movie. In particular, parts of the plot which were significant in the book have been left out of the script. This plot-thinning has had the effect of creating characters that are somewhat one-dimensional even if they look great in their dinosaur costumes.

Simon Gray, who did such a fabulous job in the first movie, plays Tyro. He is responsible for defending Earth from the evil pirate dinosaur Piratopod. Help with this mission is provided by a couple of velociraptor co-stars named Barry (Evan Green) and Kevin (Brian Scott). Piratopod has invented a solar-powered meteor magnet and intends to capture meteors from their space orbits, re-directing them onto a collision course with Earth. Tyro must mobilise the Earth Defence Team to locate and disable Piratopod's secret weapon. It's a typical 'good-guy-fights-bad-guy-and-overcomes-a-few-problems-along-the-way-while-winning-in-the-end' sort of movie. Usually this is a reasonable formula for success. However, the plot is mind-numbingly predictable, with gaps in the story that become obvious quite early on. This also means that the story tends to jolt strangely from one scene to the next.

I often use a 'spoiler alert' to warn readers when I intend to provide key details about a movie. In this case however, the story is so under-developed that there aren't many key details to reveal. You would think the director might have considered borrowing ideas from Sidle's books to make the characters more interesting - for instance Piratopod's twisted personality was actually explained as the result of traumatic events in his past. But no.

It is clearly in special effects that all the time and energy were invested in this movie, and if you love this sort of thing you will be enthralled. The views of Earth and the Moon are spectacular. I wasn't sitting in a cinema wearing 3D glasses; I was out there in space! Although the story is weak and the characters under-developed, the special effects are brilliant. They are the icing on a stale cake!

If the movie makers had followed Lillian Sidle's work more closely, this movie could have been a success. My suggestion to fans is to save your money on this movie and buy the book instead.

Reviewed by Lee Evan
Rated: PG

AnswerA: This is how the characters are portrayed in the book.
AnswerB: The actors did not have the experience to play the parts.
AnswerC: There is a lack of character development in the movie.
AnswerD: The characters are played by unknown actors in the movie.

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
Windows into the Wild
Walk into many natural history museums and you will find glass cases that seem to open onto another world: a misty rainforest, a snowy mountain slope or a billabong at sunset. These scenes are called dioramas. Although each one looks like a window, it is really a clever illusion built by a team of artists and scientists.
Creating a diorama usually happens in several stages.
First, the team studies the real place. Artists visit the location, take photographs, make sketches and collect samples of soil, leaves and rocks. Scientists check which animals and plants really belong together, and at what time of year.
Next, a painter creates the background on a curved wall at the back of the case. Because the wall curves, there are no corners to give the trick away. Distant hills and sky are painted in soft, pale colours, since faraway things look hazy to our eyes.
Then the foreground is built. This is the part closest to the glass. It holds real or carefully copied rocks, logs and soil, along with model leaves made one by one from wax, paper or plastic. Some dioramas contain thousands of handmade leaves.
The hardest job is joining the two parts. Where the real ground meets the painted wall, the colours and shapes must match exactly. If they do, visitors cannot tell where the solid ground ends and the painting begins.
Finally, preserved animals or lifelike models are put in place, and the lighting is set. Lights hidden above the case can make a scene look like early morning or late afternoon.
Some visitors today prefer screens and touch displays, and a few museums have removed their older dioramas. Yet many people still stand at the glass for minutes at a time. A good diorama lets you see an animal in its home, all in a single glance, in a way that a label or a photograph never could.

AnswerA: so the lights can be hidden behind it
AnswerB: so more animals can fit inside the case
AnswerC: so there are no corners to give the trick away
AnswerD: so visitors can see it from both sides

Subject: English
ComprehensionText:
On the Tip of My Tongue
A quiz kid called Lachlan McRae
Knew the answer but just couldn't say.
It was there on his tongue,
Like a bell left unrung,
And it came to him later that day.
You know the feeling. You are trying to remember the name of a film, a song or the kid who sat next to you in Year 2. You might even know that it starts with 'M' or has three syllables, but the word itself refuses to come out. Scientists have a name for this everyday mishap. They call it a tip-of-the-tongue moment.
In 1966, two researchers at Harvard University decided to study it. They read out dictionary definitions of rare words, such as 'sampan', and asked students to name each word. Many students got stuck partway. Often they could guess the first letter, or they came up with words that sounded similar, like 'Siam' and 'sarong'. This showed that the brain had found part of the word, but not all of it.
Since then, studies have found that most people have a tip-of-the-tongue moment about once a week. These moments become more common as people get older, and they happen most often with names.
So what should you do when a word gets stuck? Strangely, trying harder can make things worse, because your brain keeps landing on the wrong word. Many experts suggest thinking about something else. The missing word often pops up on its own, sometimes hours later, usually at a moment when it is no help at all.
My uncle Dev learned this the hard way. At a trivia night, his team needed one last answer: the name of the longest river in Australia. Dev was sure he knew it. He scrunched up his face, drummed on the table and muttered 'Mur... Mur...' until the time ran out. His team lost by one point. Halfway home in the car, he suddenly shouted 'The Murray!' so loudly that Aunty Mel nearly dropped her phone. He still blames the trivia host.

AnswerA: serious and worried
AnswerB: light-hearted and informative
AnswerC: angry and complaining

ComprehensionText:
The Same Shape Twice
Lena's art teacher had asked the class to draw 'a pattern found in nature', and by Saturday morning Lena still had a blank page. Half the class had already done zebra stripes. Spider webs were too fiddly.
'Come up Tawny Hill with me,' said Grandpa, lacing his boots. 'Patterns are easier to find when you stop looking so hard.'
The track was steep and dusty. Halfway up, Lena picked up a fallen gum leaf. A pale line ran down its middle, and thinner lines branched off it, then split again and again until they were as fine as hairs. She tucked it into her sketchbook without thinking much about it.
At the top, they sat on a flat rock. Far below, the creek wound across the flats towards the sea. Near the coast it split into two channels, then four, then a dozen silver threads that spread out like the fingers of a hand dipping into the water.
Lena frowned. Something about it tickled her memory. She opened her sketchbook, and the gum leaf slid out onto the rock. She held it up against the view. The thick middle vein, the branches, the tiny threads at the edges: the creek was drawing the very same shape across the land.
'Grandpa,' she whispered, 'the river copied the leaf.'
Grandpa chuckled. 'Or the leaf copied the river. Look behind you.'
Lena turned. A dead tree stood at the edge of the hilltop, its bare branches black against the sky. Trunk, branches, twigs, smaller twigs. The same shape again, this time reaching up instead of out.
All the way home, Lena kept finding it. In the cracks of a dried-up puddle. In the blue veins on the back of Grandpa's wrist. That night a summer storm rolled in, and as lightning forked across the clouds, she pressed her nose to the window and laughed out loud.
On Monday, Lena handed in a page divided into five boxes: a leaf, a river, a tree, a wrist and a flash of lightning. Underneath, in her neatest writing, was one word: Branches.

AnswerA: She picked it up from the dusty track.
AnswerB: She turned around to look at the dead tree.
AnswerC: She tucked it back into her sketchbook.
AnswerD: She held it up against the view.

Lena frowned. Something about it tickled her memory. She opened her sketchbook, and the gum leaf slid out onto the rock. She held it up against the view. The thick middle vein, the branches, the tiny threads at the edges: the creek was drawing the very same shape across the land.
'Grandpa,' she whispered, 'the river copied the leaf.'
Grandpa chuckled. 'Or the leaf copied the river. Look behind you.'
Lena turned. A dead tree stood at the edge of the hilltop, its bare branches black against the sky. Trunk, branches, twigs, smaller twigs. The same shape again, this time reaching up instead of out.
All the way home, Lena kept finding it. In the cracks of a dried-up puddle. In the blue veins on the back of Grandpa's wrist. That night a summer storm rolled in, and as lightning forked across the clouds, she pressed her nose to the window and laughed out loud.
On Monday, Lena handed in a page divided into five boxes: a leaf, a river, a tree, a wrist and a flash of lightning. Underneath, in her neatest writing, was one word: Branches.
